assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — Rational Exponents
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.instructions: Rational exponents. Each question has a box for every step — the root, the power, the exponent you add, the form you rewrite — and each step is checked. Answers are graded in the form asked: a "radical form" box needs a radical and an "exponential form" box a rational exponent. You have 3 tries on each Warm-Up, Classwork and Practice question, with hints. The Exit Ticket is one try with no hints.
assignment.teacherNotes: Algebra II Honors, Radicals Lesson 3 (Rational Exponents), from the district slides, TEKS A2.7G (with A.11B, the laws of exponents). Warm-Up rebuilt as readiness: integer exponent laws → negative exponents → why b^(1/n) must be the nth root. Classwork follows every slide example and Check Your Progress. Simplified means positive exponents, no fractional exponent in a denominator, reduced exponents and the smallest index. Two audited Digital SAT items from the CCMR bank sit in Practice; P7–P11 are the Honors extension (DOK 3–4), so the Honors version is ready as written. Warm-Up and Exit Ticket are generated per student and back Recovery. Slide note: the Check Your Progress ⁶√(16x²) = ∛(4x) holds for x ≥ 0; CW8 states that assumption (for every real x it is ∛(4|x|)).

sections.title: Warm-Up — From Exponent Laws to Roots

questions.prompt: Exponent laws you already know. Write each as one power of $x$ and give the exponent: $x^{ {{a}} }\cdot x^{ {{b}} }$, $(x^{ {{c}} })^{ {{d}} }$ and $\dfrac{x^{ {{e}} }}{x^{ {{f}} }}$.
directionSteps: Use the product of powers rule.
Use the power of a power rule.
Use the quotient of powers rule.
hints: Multiplying powers with the same base: add the exponents.
A power of a power: multiply the exponents.
Dividing powers with the same base: subtract the exponents.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x² · x³ equals…

steps.title: Product and quotient of powers
steps.instruction: xᵃ · xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ and xᵃ/xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ (x ≠ 0).

steps.title: Power of a power
steps.instruction: (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ. These rules still hold when the exponents are fractions.

solutionReview.headline: Add, multiply, subtract.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the exponents for a product: x^{{a}} · x^{{b}} adds them.

questions.prompt: Negative exponents. Write $ {{b}}^{-{{n}}} $ as a fraction, and write $x^{-{{k}}}$ with a positive exponent.
directionSteps: Write the first power as a fraction.
Rewrite the second power with a positive exponent.
hints: A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the positive power.
Evaluate the positive power first, then take its reciprocal.

steps.title: Negative exponent
steps.instruction: x⁻ᵃ = 1/xᵃ and 1/x⁻ᵃ = xᵃ (x ≠ 0). A negative exponent is never a negative number.

solutionReview.headline: Take the reciprocal of the positive power.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing a negative number: {{b}}^(−{{n}}) is positive.

questions.prompt: What could $b^{1/n}$ mean? If the power of a power rule still works for fractions, then $(x^{1/{{n}}})^{ {{n}} } = x^{ {{n}} \cdot \frac{1}{ {{n}} } }$. Use that to find $ {{p}}^{1/{{n}}} $, given that $ {{c}}^{ {{n}} } = {{p}} $, and decide what $b^{1/n}$ must be.
directionSteps: Multiply the exponents.
Find the number whose power is the given number.
Decide what the fractional power must be.
hints: Multiply a whole number by its reciprocal.
If raising a number to the power {{n}} gives {{p}}, that number is the one you want.
Which operation undoes raising to the nth power?

steps.title: b^(1/n)
steps.instruction: For any real b and positive integer n, b^(1/n) = ⁿ√b, except when b < 0 and n is even. 27^(1/3) = ∛27 = 3.

solutionReview.headline: A power that undoes the nth power is the nth root.
reasoning: (x^(1/{{n}}))^{{n}} = x^1 = x, so x^(1/{{n}}) is a number whose {{n}}th power is x.
solutionReview.commonError: Reading b^(1/n) as b ÷ n.

sections.title: Classwork — Rational Exponents: Rewrite, Evaluate, Simplify

questions.prompt: Properties of exponents, Examples A–C. Assume no variable equals 0. Simplify $(a^{-3})(a^2b^4)(c^{-1})$, $\dfrac{n^2}{n^{10}}$ and $\left(\dfrac{3a^3}{b^4}\right)^2$. A simplified monomial has no powers of powers, each base once, fractions in simplest form, and no negative exponents.
directionSteps: Combine the powers of each base in the first expression.
Simplify the first expression.
Simplify the second expression.
Simplify the third expression.

responses.label: In the first expression, the exponent of a is −3 + 2 =

hints: Add the exponents of the same base when multiplying.
Move any factor with a negative exponent to the other part of the fraction.
For a power of a quotient, raise every factor to the power.

steps.title: Properties of exponents
steps.instruction: Product, quotient, negative exponent, power of a power, of a product and of a quotient, and zero power (x⁰ = 1).

steps.title: Simplified monomial
steps.instruction: No powers of powers, each base once, fractions in simplest form, no negative exponents.

solutionReview.headline: Combine each base, then clear negative exponents.
reasoning: a⁻³ · a² = a⁻¹, so the first is b⁴ · a⁻¹ · c⁻¹ = b⁴/(ac).
solutionReview.commonError: Writing n² ÷ n¹⁰ = n⁵: subtract the exponents, do not divide them.

questions.prompt: Check Your Progress A–C. Assume no variable equals 0. Simplify $(x^{-2}y^{-3})(x^{-3}y^5)(z^2)$, $\dfrac{h^6}{h^{-2}}$ and $\left(\dfrac{6r^2}{3s^3}\right)^2$.
directionSteps: Choose the simplified form of the first expression.
Simplify the second expression.
Simplify the third expression.
hints: Add the exponents of each base.
Subtracting a negative exponent adds it.
Simplify 6/3 inside the parentheses first.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. h⁶ / h⁻² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Same rules, mind the signs.
reasoning: x⁻²⁻³ = x⁻⁵ and y⁻³⁺⁵ = y², so the product is y²z²/x⁵.
solutionReview.commonError: Choosing 4r⁴/s⁹: (s³)² is s⁶, not s⁹.

questions.prompt: Radical and exponential forms. $b^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{b}$. Write $a^{1/7}$ in radical form and $\sqrt{w}$ in exponential form. Then write $a^{1/3}$ in radical form and $\sqrt[5]{x}$ in exponential form.
directionSteps: Write the first power in radical form.
Write the square root in exponential form.
Do the same for the last two.
hints: The denominator of the exponent is the index of the radical.
A square root has index 2.

solutionReview.headline: The denominator is the index.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing √(a³) for a^(1/3): the 3 is the index, not a power.

questions.prompt: Evaluate expressions with rational exponents. Evaluate $49^{-1/2}$ and $32^{2/5}$, one step at a time. Then evaluate $25^{-1/2}$ and $16^{3/4}$.
directionSteps: Take the root first.
Then apply the power or the reciprocal.
Evaluate the last two the same way.
hints: A negative exponent means the reciprocal.
Another method: write the base as a power of a smaller number, then multiply the exponents.
Write 16 as a power of a smaller number, then multiply the exponents.

steps.title: Method 1
steps.instruction: Take the root first, then the power: 32^(2/5) = (⁵√32)² = 2² = 4.

steps.title: Method 2
steps.instruction: Write the base as a power and multiply exponents: 32^(2/5) = (2⁵)^(2/5) = 2² = 4.

solutionReview.headline: Root first, then power; a negative exponent is a reciprocal.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 49^(−1/2) = −7: a negative exponent gives a reciprocal, not a negative number.

questions.prompt: Rational exponents: $b^{x/y} = \sqrt[y]{b^x} = \left(\sqrt[y]{b}\right)^x$. Evaluate $27^{2/3}$ and $(-8)^{2/3}$. Then decide whether $(-16)^{3/2}$ is a real number, and explain.
directionSteps: Evaluate the first power, root first.
Evaluate the second power, root first.
Decide whether the third power is real and explain.

responses.label: (−16)^(3/2) is…
options: not a real number: the root is even and the base is negative (in the complex numbers it is −64i)
a real number, because 3/2 is positive
responses.answer: not a real number: the root is even and the base is negative (in the complex numbers it is −64i)

hints: The denominator of the exponent is the root, the numerator is the power.
An odd root of a negative number is real; an even root is not.
Find ∛(−8) first, then square it.

solutionReview.headline: Root first: the index decides whether a negative base works.
reasoning: (−8)^(2/3) = (∛(−8))² = (−2)² = 4: the root is odd, so it is real.
(−16)^(3/2) = (√(−16))³: an even root of a negative number is not real (4i, so (4i)³ = −64i).
solutionReview.commonError: Calling (−8)^(2/3) not real: the root is a cube root, which accepts a negative base.

questions.prompt: WEIGHTLIFTING. The formula $M = 512 - 146{,}230B^{-8/5}$ estimates the maximum total mass $M$ (kilograms) a weightlifter of mass $B$ kilograms can lift. Find $M$ for a lifter of 168 kilograms, one step at a time. Then find $M$ for a lifter of 80 kilograms. Use a calculator.
directionSteps: Find the power with a positive exponent.
Divide.
Subtract from 512.
Find the maximum for the second lifter.

responses.label: For B = 80 kilograms, M is about…

hints: B^(−8/5) = 1/B^(8/5), so multiplying by it divides by B^(8/5).
On a calculator, enter the exponent 8/5 in parentheses.
Subtract the quotient from 512 last.

solutionReview.headline: A negative exponent divides.
solutionReview.commonError: Typing 168^8/5 without parentheses: the calculator raises to the 8th power and then divides by 5.

questions.prompt: Simplify expressions with rational exponents. Simplify $y^{1/7}\cdot y^{4/7}$ and $x^{-2/3}$; a simplified answer has no negative exponents and no fractional exponent in a denominator. Then simplify $x^{1/5}\cdot x^{2/5}$ and $y^{-3/4}$.
directionSteps: Add the exponents of the first product.
Rewrite the second power with a positive exponent.
Clear the fractional exponent from the denominator.
Simplify the last two the same way.
hints: Add the fractions in the exponents.
Multiply the top and bottom by the power that makes the denominator’s exponent a whole number.
Exponents add when you multiply: two thirds plus one third is one.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x^(2/3) · x^(1/3) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Add exponents; clear the fractional exponent from the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving 1/x^(2/3): no fractional exponent may stay in a denominator.

questions.prompt: Simplify radical expressions with rational exponents. Simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt[6]{16}}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$ and $\sqrt[6]{4x^4}$. Then simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt[4]{4}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\sqrt[6]{16x^2}$. Assume $x$ is positive.
directionSteps: Write each radical as a power of two.
Simplify the first quotient.
Reduce the index of the second radical.
Simplify the last two the same way.
hints: Reduce the fraction in the exponent before writing a radical.

solutionReview.headline: Exponents make different indices comparable.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving ⁶√(4x⁴): the index is not as small as it can be.

questions.prompt: A conjugate with exponents. Simplify $\dfrac{y^{1/2} + 1}{y^{1/2} - 1}$ by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator. Then simplify $\dfrac{x^{1/2} - 1}{x^{1/2} + 1}$.
directionSteps: Name the conjugate of the denominator.
Multiply the denominator by its conjugate.
Simplify the first quotient.
Choose the simplified form of the second quotient.
hints: A conjugate changes the sign between the two terms.
Square the numerator by multiplying it by itself.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate over itself.
reasoning: So the quotient is (y + 2y^(1/2) + 1)/(y − 1); the second is (x − 2x^(1/2) + 1)/(x − 1).
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring y^(1/2) + 1 as y + 1: the middle term 2y^(1/2) is missing.

questions.prompt: Is it simplified? An expression with rational exponents is simplified when it has no negative exponents, no exponents that are not positive integers in a denominator, it is not a complex fraction, and the index of any remaining radical is as small as possible. Decide whether each is simplified, and name the rule it breaks if it is not.
directionSteps: Check each expression against the four rules.
Decide whether it is simplified.
Name the rule it breaks, if any.

responses.label: x^(−1/2)
options: Not simplified: it has a negative exponent
Not simplified: it is a complex fraction
Not simplified: the index can be smaller
responses.answer: Not simplified: it has a negative exponent

responses.label: 1 / y^(2/3)
options: Not simplified: a fractional exponent is in the denominator
Not simplified: it has a negative exponent
Not simplified: the index can be smaller
responses.answer: Not simplified: a fractional exponent is in the denominator

responses.label: ⁸√(x⁴)
options: Not simplified: the index can be smaller
Not simplified: it has a negative exponent
Not simplified: it is a complex fraction
responses.answer: Not simplified: the index can be smaller

responses.label: (x^(1/3))/x
options: Not simplified: it has a negative exponent
Not simplified: a fractional exponent is in the denominator
Not simplified: the index can be smaller

responses.label: Write ⁸√(x⁴) in simplest form (x positive)

hints: Test each rule one at a time.
A whole-number exponent in a denominator is allowed.
x^(4/8) can be reduced.

solutionReview.headline: Four rules, one at a time.
reasoning: x^(−1/2) has a negative exponent; 1/y^(2/3) has a fractional exponent in the denominator.
⁸√(x⁴) = x^(4/8) = x^(1/2) = √x, a smaller index. (x^(1/3))/x breaks no rule.
solutionReview.answerSummary: a, b, c not simplified; d simplified; ⁸√(x⁴) = √x
solutionReview.commonError: Calling (x^(1/3))/x unsimplified: the denominator’s exponent is a positive integer.

directionSteps: Take the root first.

hints: The denominator of the exponent is the root.

directionSteps: Rewrite with a positive exponent.
Take the root, then the power.
hints: A negative exponent means the reciprocal.
Evaluate the positive power first.

solutionReview.headline: Reciprocal of the positive power.

questions.prompt: Rewrite each form. Write $\sqrt[{{n}}]{x^{ {{m}} }}$ in exponential form, and write $y^{ {{a}}/{{b}} }$ in radical form.
directionSteps: Write the radical in exponential form.
Write the power in radical form.

solutionReview.commonError: Switching the numerator and the denominator.

questions.prompt: Simplify $x^{ {{a}}/{{n}} }\cdot x^{ {{b}}/{{n}} }$. Write the answer with a rational exponent.
directionSteps: Add the exponents.
Reduce the exponent if you can.
hints: Multiplying powers with the same base: add the exponents.
The exponents have the same denominator.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. a^(1/5) · a^(2/5) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Add the exponents.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the exponents instead of adding them.

questions.prompt: Simplify $ {{k}}x^{-{{a}}/{{n}}} $ so it has no negative exponent and no fractional exponent in a denominator.
directionSteps: Rewrite with a positive exponent.
Clear the fractional exponent from the denominator.
hints: Move the power to the denominator to make the exponent positive.
Multiply the top and bottom by the power that brings the denominator’s exponent up to a whole number.

solutionReview.headline: Positive exponent, then a whole-number exponent below.

questions.prompt: WEIGHTLIFTING. The maximum total mass $M$ (kilograms) a weightlifter of mass $B$ kilograms can lift is about $M = 512 - 146{,}230B^{-8/5}$. Find $M$ for a lifter of {{B}} kilograms. Use a calculator.
directionSteps: Find the power with a positive exponent.
Divide.

hints: A negative exponent divides: 146,230 · B^(−8/5) = 146,230 ÷ B^(8/5).
Put the exponent 8/5 in parentheses on the calculator.

solutionReview.headline: Divide by the positive power, then subtract.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by {{B}}^(8/5) instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — model with a table. A cube with volume V cubic centimeters has surface area S = 6V^(2/3) square centimeters. Complete the table, write V^(2/3) in radical form, and describe what happens to S when V is multiplied by 8. Explain why.
directionSteps: Find the surface area for each volume in the table.
Write the power in radical form.
Describe and explain what happens when the volume is multiplied by 8.

responses.label: When V is multiplied by 8, S is multiplied by
Why?
options: The surface area does not depend on the volume

hints: Each volume is a perfect cube: find its cube root, square it, then multiply by 6.
The denominator 3 is the index of the radical.
Use the power of a product: (ab)^(2/3) = a^(2/3) · b^(2/3).

solutionReview.headline: Root, power, multiply by 6.
reasoning: Multiplying V by 8 multiplies V^(2/3) by 8^(2/3) = 4 (the edge doubles, so each face is 4 times as large).
solutionReview.commonError: Expecting S to be multiplied by 8 too: area grows like the square of the edge, volume like its cube.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — when do the exponent laws hold? Ana writes $(-8)^{2/6} = (-8)^{1/3} = -2$. Ben writes $(-8)^{2/6} = \sqrt[6]{(-8)^2} = \sqrt[6]{64} = 2$. Evaluate each step, decide who made the error, and explain why.
directionSteps: Evaluate the root that Ben uses.
Evaluate the cube root that Ana uses.
Decide who made the error.
Explain why.

responses.label: The two answers differ because…
options: reducing 2/6 to 1/3 changes the value when the base is negative: the exponent laws hold for nonnegative bases
responses.answer: reducing 2/6 to 1/3 changes the value when the base is negative: the exponent laws hold for nonnegative bases

responses.label: So, for a negative base, a rational exponent must be written in…
options: a form with an even denominator

hints: Square −8 first, then take the sixth root.
An odd root of a negative number is negative.
Which step changed a power of a negative base?

solutionReview.headline: Exponent laws need a nonnegative base.
reasoning: Both computations are correct; the expressions differ because reducing 2/6 to 1/3 for a negative base is not allowed — (bᵐ)^(1/n) = (b^(1/n))ᵐ needs b ≥ 0 when n is even.
So b^(x/y) is defined with x/y in lowest terms: (−8)^(1/3) = −2.
solutionReview.answerSummary: They differ; write the exponent in lowest terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Applying (bᵐ)^(1/n) = (b^(1/n))ᵐ to a negative base with an even n.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — different indices. Assume $x$ is positive. Simplify $\sqrt{x}\cdot\sqrt[3]{x}$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt[4]{x^3}}{\sqrt{x}}$ by writing each radical with a rational exponent.
directionSteps: Write each radical as a power of x.
Add or subtract the exponents.
Write each answer in radical form.
hints: Use a common denominator to add the exponents.

solutionReview.headline: Common denominators combine different indices.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the radicands and keeping one index: √x · ∛x is not √(x²) or ∛(x²).

questions.prompt: Honors extension — reduce the index. Assume $x$ and $y$ are positive. Simplify $\sqrt[8]{16x^4y^{12}}$.
directionSteps: Write the radicand as a power of a monomial.
Write the root with a rational exponent and reduce it.
Write the answer in simplest radical form.
hints: 16 = 2⁴; divide each exponent by 4.
Pull the perfect square out of 2xy³.

solutionReview.headline: Rational exponents reduce the index.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at √(2xy³): y² is a perfect-square factor still under the radical.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — compare without a calculator. Which is greater, $2^{1/2}$ or $3^{1/3}$? Raise both to the sixth power to decide, and justify.
directionSteps: Raise the first number to the sixth power.
Raise the second number to the sixth power.
Decide which is greater and justify.

responses.label: Which is greater?
options: It cannot be decided without a calculator

responses.label: Why does comparing sixth powers work?
options: Both numbers are positive, and for positive numbers raising to the sixth power keeps their order
The sixth power of every number is positive
responses.answer: Both numbers are positive, and for positive numbers raising to the sixth power keeps their order

hints: Use the power of a power rule: multiply the exponents.
6 is a common multiple of 2 and 3.

solutionReview.headline: A common power removes both roots.
reasoning: 8 < 9, and sixth powers keep the order of positive numbers, so 3^(1/3) > 2^(1/2).
solutionReview.commonError: Comparing the exponents 1/2 > 1/3 and concluding 2^(1/2) is greater: the bases differ too.

questions.prompt: For $x>0$, $\sqrt{x^n}=x{{k|pow}}\sqrt{x{{m|pow}}}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. What is the value of $n$?

optionRationales.{{n}}: Right: moving x^{{k}} back under the square root doubles its exponent, so n = 2({{k}}) + {{m}}.
optionRationales.{{dNoDouble}}: This adds the outside exponent as it is: under a square root, x^{{k}} becomes x^(2·{{k}}).
optionRationales.{{dDoubledBoth}}: This also doubles the exponent that is already under the root; only the outside factor’s exponent doubles.
optionRationales.{{dDoubledWrong}}: This doubles the exponent under the root instead of the one outside it.

solutionReview.headline: Move the outside factor back under the radical.
solutionReview.commonError: Moving the outside power under the radical without doubling its exponent: xᵏ outside a square root is x²ᵏ inside it.

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression and preserve equivalence.
supportHints: Combine like terms, distribute, factor, or simplify the radical structure as appropriate.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x² · √x as one radical equals, for x > 0…

optionRationales.{{n}}: Right: a power of a power multiplies, giving {{p}}·{{r}} over {{q}}, and dividing subtracts {{s}} over {{q}}.
optionRationales.{{dAdded}}: This adds the denominator’s exponent; dividing powers of x subtracts exponents.
optionRationales.{{dNoSubtraction}}: This applies the power rule but skips the division: subtract the denominator’s exponent too.
optionRationales.{{dAddedExponents}}: This adds {{p}} and {{r}}; raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents.

solutionReview.headline: Apply the power rule, then the quotient rule.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the exponents for a power of a power, or adding instead of subtracting the exponent of the denominator.

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression rather than changing its value.
supportHints: Look for a factoring or exponent-law relationship that preserves equivalence.
